concepts.name: The three structural signatures
concepts.summary: Alongside the five functional properties, the paper claims the J-space shows three structural marks of a workspace: it operates only in a band of layers, it is limited in capacity, and its vectors compose unusually broadly with the model's weights.
concepts.explanation: The five workspace-like properties are functional: they describe what the model can do with these representations. The paper makes a second, separate set of claims about how the J-space is arranged inside the network. First, it is confined to a band of depth: J-space content is essentially absent in the early layers, emerges over a relatively narrow transition into a stable middle regime, and gives way in the final layers to representations tied to the imminent output. Second, within that band it is limited in capacity, accounting for only a small fraction of the activation variance at any position, with most representational features lying outside it. Third, it is mechanistically privileged: J-lens vectors compose with the input weights of downstream MLP and attention components, and with upstream weights, far more broadly than other directions do, which is what one would expect of a format many circuits read from and write to. These are the "some structural ones" the paper concedes when it declines to claim the full brain architecture; each maps onto a property global workspace theory ascribes to the brain, and each is established in its own later section.

concepts.name: Emerged, not built in
concepts.summary: The paper stresses that nothing in the transformer architecture provides a workspace module; whatever workspace-like organization it finds appeared in ordinary training of ordinary models.
concepts.explanation: Earlier proposals treated a global workspace as a design target, adding a workspace-like bottleneck module to a network on purpose. This paper studies existing, widely used language models, where no such module was specified: the transformer has no separable input processors, no recurrent loops, and no architectural bottleneck through which content must pass. The paper opens by granting that a workspace therefore is not obviously to be expected, and argues only that one would be useful, since a common representational format lets an intermediate result be written once and read by many downstream processes. Its reading of the finding is that the functional organization associated with conscious access is not tied to biological implementation but is a solution learning systems converge on under the right computational pressures. That reading is an interpretation rather than a demonstration: the experiments show the structure is present in trained models, not which training pressures produced it.
